It's the trans-pacific partnership. It's similar to NAFTA in the way that it is a deal between many nations dealing with trade. This will help corporations while doing very little for the people. From my understanding there is some stiff copyright laws snuck in that are very similar to SOPA. It will help offshore more jobs to foreign countries, raise drug prices, and will allow for more pollution by corporations. (http://www.citizen.org/TPP) However if you decide to read about it from the white house website, it paints a completely different and very rosy picture of how the deal will increase the production and export of Made In America products as well as make foreign pollution laws up to par with those of the United States.

Its a trade agreement between pacific rim countries that will decrease trade barriers, standardize IP laws and government-corporation arbitration. Here's a link of debunked populist notions about TTP.

This comic explains things very well.

Short short version:

"Free Trade" treaties like this have been around for a long time. The problem is, the United States, and indeed most of the world, has had practically free trade since the 50s. What these new treaties do is allow corporations to manipulate currency and stock markets, to trade goods for capital, resulting in money moving out of an economy never to return, and override the governments of nations that they operate in because they don't like policy.

For example, Australia currently has a similar treaty with Hong Kong. They recently passed a "plain packaging" law for cigarettes, they cannot advertise to children anymore. The cigarette companies don't like this, so they went to a court in Hong Kong, and they sued Australia for breaking international law by making their advertising tactics illegal. This treaty has caused Australia to give up their sovereignty to mega-corporations.

Another thing these treaties do is allow companies to relocate whenever they like. This means that, when taxes are going to be raised, corporations can just get up and leave, which means less jobs, and even less revenue for the government.

The TPP has some particularly egregious clauses concerning intellectual property. It requires that signatory companies grant patents on things like living things that should not be patentable, and not deny patents based on evidence that the invention is not new or revolutionary. In other words, if the TPP was in force eight years ago, Apple would have gotten the patent they requested on rectangles.
This is a pretty good beginners explanation of TPP and "Free Trade" In general.

Is there anything I should know? Where I live it gets to a low of -5 a couple of times a year. Will I be able to handle the cold? I would like to continue my trade of cabinet making will I freeze my arse off doing this or are work shops heated? Any areas I should avoid? Would I need my own car or is public transport well done?
I'm thinking of moving to Toronto from Australia for 2 years.

You should be able to find a place downtown close to subways or other transit lines, so no car should be requiered. We have decent transit, not as good as much of Europe, but if you live close to the lines it is ok.

In the winter it usually stays above -15, but sometimes can dip below -20, and worse with windchill. However i would assume most work places are heated for health and safety reasons.

Try to stick to 'downtown'. You'll have more to do, and waste less time commuting. If you look at the subway, try to stick between Jane and coxwell on the bloor line, and south of eglington on the Yonge liNe. Further out then that and i feel you lose some of the big city appeal

One thing to note, Canada may be sliding into recession, so finding a job might prove difficult. Line something up before you get here.

Hey there, the cold will numb your skin and make it fall off if you are not careful. You will need real winter clothes. Like $100 boots, $80 winter coat, long underwear, touque, scarves, mits... For like 4-5 months... anyways.... Summer though, sweet bliss! Living right in downtown Toronto is expensive, and great in the summer. You will find more industry on the outskirts of the GTA - Mississauga, Brampton, Vaughan, Concord etc. A car will help you a lot, as public transport here pretty much sucks.
Learn the rules of baseball, basketball, CFL and hockey.

Good stuff in here already. Transit can be annoying at times but definitely gets you around town. I would add that a lot of people bike around downtown, if you're into that sort of thing. There's more and more bike lanes popping up lately.

Though I'd also classify 'downtown' not going as far out as skiffy says, but you can check out maps when looking for a place and see where works for you. Places to avoid would be Jane-Finch, Sherbourne-Jarvis, and Regent Park. There's a couple bad spots but luckily, only a couple. Toronto is actually very safe, given its size and the fact that it's the biggest city in the country.

The downtown core (between Spadina-Church, maybe?) is expensive to live, but there are lots of great neighbourhoods around town to check out. Off the top of my head I'd recommend any of Leslieville, High Park, the Annex, the Junction, Little Italy, Parkdale, and West Queen West (near Trinity Bellwoods Park). There's more good spots, these would just be my initial suggestions.

The last two winters have been frigid even by Toronto's standards, but generally it hovers around the -10 to -15 mark, with the occasional dip into the -20s (or lower) just a couple times a winter. The windchill is ultimately what makes it worse so just make sure you bundle up. You can definitely survive it, but do make sure you come with some real winter jackets (or buy a big one when you get here, there's plenty around these parts)

High Park isn't the cheapest place in town, but if you can find a spot to rent in there that works with your budget I'd say go for it! It's a really nice part of town. The Junction borders High Park as well and is also nice, so you could always check that out. High Park is not in an industrial area by any means, but it is on the subway line which is good, and not too far from the highways (should you need to hop into a car and drive off somewhere). If you don't want to buy a car there are a few car share services around town, in case that works if/when necessary for you to jump on the road: Zipcar, Autoshare, car2go.

I have a small suggestion. Don't rush into taking the first apartment you find. I recommend renting out a cheap airbnb place for a few weeks while you properly feel out the markets. Toronto is expensive, but it has unexpectedly affordable spots if you look patiently enough. Or if not, at least be sure it's a neighbourhood you can really feel at home in.

I would say that it will be expensive to find a place in Toronto with a workshop. As for it being heated, that will be up to your budget. Be prepared to pay somewhat dearly for that (In fact, considering Toronto, you'll pay dearly just for the space to work in even if it's an unheated garage). I think you might find it difficult to transport supplies for cabinet making without a vehicle, though perhaps in Toronto you'll find places that deliver (You can always rent a vehicle, but you will need to have a driver's license. You will lose your right to use your Australian license within the 2 year period, and I imagine you might have trouble renting a van at a home improvement store on a foreign license.) Public transit in Toronto is fine. Fortunately Australia has reciprocal agreements with Ontario so getting an Ontario license will be simplified.
